text:
Dear Santa Claus:
Papa would like you to bring him a new cap and new rubbers. Papa did not have time to write, so I wrote for him. Please send me a doll for myself.
MAYBELLE.
title: Papa did not have time to write
author: Maybelle
story: Printed by the Washington Evening Star on 20 December 1908 among children’s letters to Santa Claus that never reached him and piled up at the Dead Letter Office.

source.name: Evening Star (Washington, D.C.), 20 December 1908, 'Post Office glutted with Santa Claus letters from the children' (feature by Frederic Bulkeley Hyde), via Chronicling America, Library of Congress
source.licence: Public domain (US newspaper published 1908; LOC: "believes that the newspapers in Chronicling America are in the public domain or have no known copyright restrictions")

rights.basis: US: first printed in a US newspaper in 1908 (before 1931). EU/UK: printed anonymously in 1908 (the child is identified only by the first name 'Maybelle'; no surname or address), so not identifiable; anonymous work published before 1956. Transcribed from the 1908 page image at the Library of Congress, not from a modern edition. The feature carries the line 'Text and Illustrations Copyright, 1908, by Frederic Bulkeley Hyde'; that US copyright has long expired and his prose is not quoted. Letter year: written for Christmas 1908 or shortly before (the article is dated 20 Dec 1908). Signature printed in capitals ('MAYBELLE'), rendered here as 'Maybelle'.

text:
My Dear Madam:—
William has written you quite a long letter, yet I thought I could not let this opportunity pass without writing you a few lines …

My children are as fat as pigs: Granderson is nearly as broad as he is long …

In the morning I get up early to milk my cow, feed my chickens, &c. The last time I churned I had to put warm water in the churn to make the butter come.
Yours humbly,
Rosebell Burke.
title: Butter in the churn
author: Rosebell Burke (Rosabella Burke)

writer.heritage: Liberian settler (African American emigrant from Virginia)
writer.basis: Printed as 'From Mrs. Burke' under 'Letters from Liberia'; the 1854 emigrant roll lists William Burke, 36, and 'Rosabella, wife, 34' of Fairfax County, Va., freed ('Em.') by Col. R. E. Lee, with their four children.

recipient: Mrs. Mary C. Lee, Arlington, Virginia
story: Sent from Clay-Ashland with her husband’s letter of 20 February 1859 to Mary Custis Lee, whose family had freed the Burkes before they emigrated; she let the Colonization Society print both that July.

source.name: The African Repository (American Colonization Society, Washington), vol. 35 (July 1859), p. 216; Internet Archive scan, page image read
source.licence: Public domain (text printed 1859); scan from Internet Archive

rights.basis: Printed 1859 (US: before 1931). The Society's printed emigrant roll (African Repository, vol. 30, Jan. 1854) lists 'Rosabella [Burke], wife, 34', so she was born about 1819 and, even after a life of 120 years, dead by 1939: more than 70 years ago.

text:
Diario CRITICA. Señor:
papito dice siempre que Vd. sabe todo. Si sabe la dirección de los reyes mayor, haga el favor de llevarle esta carta. Así yo lo quiero a usted mucho, mucho.

Señores Reyes Magos: acuérdensen de la Pochi. Tráiganme muchas cosas, todas las que están en el diario. No se vayan a equivocar de casa. … Muchos besitos para mis queridos reyes.
(Pochi Mari Elena)
title: Papito says you know everything
author: Unknown (signed 'Pochi Mari Elena'; first names only)
recipient: the editor of Crítica, and through him the Reyes Magos
story: Sent to the Buenos Aires daily Crítica with a plea to forward it to the Three Kings, and printed in the paper on 28 December 1923 under the headline ‘Hermosa carta de una criatura’.

source.name: Diario Crítica, 28 Dec 1923 (no. 4028), Internet Archive scan BNA_S001181802_19231228N04028 (image 9)
source.licence: Public domain (printed 1923); no licence statement on the archive.org item

rights.basis: US: first printed 1923, before 1931. EU: printed anonymously before 1956: signed only with a nickname and first names ('Pochi Mari Elena'), no surname, so the writer is not identifiable. The printed letter also gives a street address ('Treinta y tres 2277'); that sentence is cut from our excerpt. Transcription is ours, read from the 1923 page image (pre-1931 printed text).

text:
Je saisis l’occasion qui se présente pour te donner, mon cher frère, de mes nouvelles. …

Je finis par t’engager à me donner plus souvent de tes nouvelles, et de te rappeler que nous sommes ici comme en exil, pour nos péchés sans doute ; mais patience ; — lorsqu’ils seront expiés, nous irons en paradis, et ce lieu pour moi n’est autre chose que ma bastide de Toulon, ma femme, mes enfans et toi que j’aimerai toujours.
Adieu ; je t’embrasse et suis pour la vie,
Ton tendre frère,
C. Fabregue
title: Paradise is my house in Toulon
author: C. Fabregue
recipient: his brother, Citizen Fabregue, aide-commissaire aboard the frigate la Mantoue at Alexandria
story: Sent from Cairo to his brother’s frigate in August 1798, it was intercepted by Nelson’s fleet and printed in London in 1799 instead of being delivered.

source.name: Correspondance intime de l'armée d'Égypte interceptée par la croisière anglaise, ed. Lorédan Larchey (Paris: R. Pincebourde, 1866), pp. 121-124
source.licence: Public domain (printed 1799 and 1866)

rights.basis: First printed 1799 in London (Copies of Original Letters from the Army of General Bonaparte in Egypt, Part the Second, J. Wright, French text with English translation; IA copy https://archive.org/details/bim_eighteenth-century_copies-of-original-lette_1799_1) and the same year in Paris (Correspondance de l'armee francaise en Egypte, Garnery, an VII; https://archive.org/details/32882019067670-correspondanced); text quoted from Larchey's 1866 Paris reprint (public domain). US: printed before 1931. EU: the writer was an adult serving in Egypt in 1798, so born before c.1780 and certainly dead long before 1956. No modern transcription used, so no publication right arises. The 1799 printing adds an editor's footnote marker after 'bastide' (explaining the word); it is not part of the letter and is omitted.

text:
Good-morning, my dear Postmistress!
I feel very well acquainted with you, though I have never had the pleasure of seeing you. … I have a very pretty little Angora cat, as white as snow. She is very funny, and her name is Lilly. … In the morning she jumps into the bed and begins to tickle my feet … I forgot to tell you that I am a little Cuban girl, and do not know English very well yet.
Maria Dolores C.
title: Lilly the Angora cat
author: Unknown (signed 'Maria Dolores C.')

writer.basis: 'I forgot to tell you that I am a little Cuban girl.'

recipient: The Postmistress of Harper's Young People, New York
story: Printed in the Post-office Box of Harper’s Young People on 19 February 1884, with the Postmistress’s reply: ‘I shall be glad to hear from you again.’

source.name: Harper's Young People, vol. V (1883–84), 19 February 1884, p. 255; Internet Archive scan harpersyoungpeop00newy1884 (text read from the page image; the OCR is unreliable)
source.licence: Public domain (printed in the 1880s); Internet Archive scan of the New York Public Library copy, marked NOT_IN_COPYRIGHT

rights.basis: Printed 1884 (before 1931). Published before 1956 with the writer identified only by first name(s) and initial(s), so the writer is not identifiable and the letter counts as published anonymously. The child's own death year is unknown.

text:
Dear Mother:—
I take this opportunity of writing you these few lines, hoping they may find you and all enquiring friends in as good health, as they leave me and my husband. Charles, my son, is quite well. … We have night-church as well as four times on Sabbath-day. I have to attend Sunday School, as I am one of the principal teachers. …

Abram Rogers’ daughter Mary, got married to Mr. Cooper last Wednesday night. …
I am your affectionate daughter till death,
Martha Snetter.
title: News for mother from Monrovia
author: Martha Snetter

writer.basis: The African Repository calls her 'a female emigrant from Charleston' writing from Monrovia, Liberia.

story: Martha Snetter, an emigrant from Charleston, wrote this to her mother from Monrovia on 26 February 1834; the African Repository printed it that July to answer a returned colonist’s report that she was desperate to come home.

source.name: The African Repository and Colonial Journal, vol. X, no. 5 (July 1834), p. 154; Internet Archive (Serials in Microfilm) scan, page image read
source.licence: Public domain (printed in the 1830s). No licence statement on the IA item; nothing in it is newly published.

rights.basis: US: printed 1834. EU: a married woman with a son, teaching Sunday school in Monrovia in 1834, so born before about 1816; dead long before 1956. Text checked against the page image (the OCR garbles 'Abram' and runs words together).

text:
My Dear Father,
I write these few lines to you, hoping to find you in good health, as, thank God, it leaves us at present. … I was confined, and that was on the 3rd. of June. … It is a fine boy, and goes on well. I am happy to tell you, that America is quite as good as we expected to find it. … there is one great comfort here; we have as much wood as we like to burn. … I remain your affectionate daughter,
Ann Thomas.
title: It is a fine boy
author: Ann Thomas
recipient: her father, Thomas Puttock, at Stroud Green, Kirdford, Sussex
story: Written in October 1832; her son was born on 3 June, four days before the family landed after nine weeks at sea; printed with other emigrants’ letters by the Petworth Emigration Committee in 1833.

source.name: Emigration: Letters from Sussex Emigrants, who sailed from Portsmouth, in April 1832, on board the ships Lord Melville and Eveline, for Upper Canada (Petworth: John Phillips, 1833); Canadiana CIHM 35220 scan on Internet Archive; text transcribed by us from the page images
source.licence: Public domain (printed 1833); scan carries no item rights statement

rights.basis: Printed at Petworth in 1833 (before 1931). Ann Thomas was writing in 1832, so was born before 1836 (a married woman with a child, so born before c.1815); death year unknown but certainly before 1956 (allowing a life of 120 years). The editors say the letters are 'faithfully given in the very words of the writers', with only the spelling corrected.

text:
Mi estimado Sor.
… Quando Don Santiago estubo en esta Capital le suplique me hiciera el favor de mandarme con la primer conducta 2 asadones delos mejores que V. tenga y una hacha de la mismas circunstancias. … reciba V espreciones de José Erasmo quien siempre que me escribe pone aV. y a Don Santiago mil espreciones, recibiendolas V. y Don Santiago delos niños y mias mande quato guste asu servidora que decea verlos y S. M. B.
Maria Josefa Agustina Bezerri
title: Two good hoes and an axe
author: Maria Josefa Agustina Bezerri (headed 'Mrs. Erasmo Seguin'; María Josefa Becerra)
recipient: Stephen F. Austin ('Sor. D. Estevan F. Austin'); 'Don Santiago' is his brother, whom Austin calls 'mi hermano Don Santiago' in letters printed in the same volume
story: Kept among Stephen F. Austin’s own papers (Austin endorsed it ‘Letter from Mrs. Erasmo Seguin’) and printed from them in 1924 in The Austin Papers, edited by Eugene C. Barker.

source.name: The Austin Papers, ed. Eugene C. Barker, Part 1 (Annual Report of the American Historical Association for the Year 1919, vol. II; Washington: Government Printing Office, 1924), p. 767
source.licence: Public domain: US federal government publication (GPO, 1924), printed before 1931; Internet Archive microfilm scan, no rights statement

rights.basis: First printed 1924 (before 1931), in a US Government Printing Office volume. EU: she married Erasmo Seguín and was the mother of Juan N. Seguín, born 1806 (Wikipedia, 'Erasmo Seguín' and 'Juan Seguín'), so she was born before about 1790 and was dead long before 1956. Spelling is the edition's literal transcription; the superscript abbreviation 'Dⁿ' is expanded to 'Don', nothing else changed.

text:
Mine kære, uforglemmelige Præstefolk!
… Saa vil jeg fortælle, at Jens Andreas Thorhave har købt et lille Hus nord i Barkær; der kan godt holdes en Ko … først i Maj blev han borgerlig viet med en ordentlig Pige; hun er 20 Aar, hendes Forældre bor i Gøttrup, de kan holde en Ko. …

Kære Venner! Der er noget forkert ved mit Skriveri, men skriver jeg ikke, faar jeg jo ingen Breve, og det er en stor Opmuntring for mig paa mine gamle Dage.
Eders Margrethe.
title: Village news, measured in cows
author: Margrethe (Margrethe Pedersen, 'Gammelmo'r i Vust')
recipient: Pastor Georg Brahm and his wife Harriet, old friends, at Seden near Odense
story: Written by a farmer’s widow of 81 in Vust to her pastor friends on Funen; after her death her son had her letters privately printed for the family around 1915.

source.name: Danmarks Breve (Royal Danish Library text portal), 'Breve fra Gammelmo'r i Vust …', letter of 5 Aug 1892 (text checked against the facsimile pages 8–10)
source.licence: Public domain (KB statement)

rights.basis: Written 5 Aug 1892. Privately printed c.1914–15 (foreword dated Nov 1914; no printed date seen), so in the US it passes as a printing before 1931; if that private printing doesn't count as publication, it still passes, as a letter first made public online by the Royal Danish Library by a writer who died in 1902. EU: the writer died in 1902; the KB release carries a public-domain statement, which also covers the publication-right question. Long passages on illness and a child's death are left out; the last paragraph is her own postscript.

text:
My Dear Josephine,
I wish you a Merry Christmas, and christmas Gift. … I have had some kisses to day from the ladies, as christman Gifts. but I have not had one from you … Miss Elina Syfacx has gott married to A Mr. Reves of Virginia I arrived her to late for the wedding, but I have some of the wedding cake—and I send you a piece of it—so when you see this cake, think of me, and your wedding day …
Your Most Devoted Lover &c
C. A. Stewart
title: A piece of the wedding cake
author: C. A. Stewart

writer.basis: Woodson introduces it: 'Love letters written by Negroes before the Civil War are both interesting and valuable … the following are sufficient to show the importance of such documents'.

story: Written in Washington on Christmas Day 1850 to Miss Josephine Jameson in Philadelphia; Carter G. Woodson printed it in 1926 as one of the few love letters by Black writers from before the Civil War that he had found.

source.name: Carter G. Woodson (ed.), The Mind of the Negro as Reflected in Letters Written During the Crisis, 1800–1860 (Washington: Association for the Study of Negro Life and History, 1926); Internet Archive scan of the State Library of Pennsylvania copy, page images read
source.licence: Public domain in the US (published 1926; US term expired 1 January 2022). No licence statement on the IA item; the letters themselves pass by date (see rights).

rights.basis: US: first printed January 1926 and in the 1926 book. EU: an adult courting by letter in 1850 who writes of 'me and my family', so born before about 1832; dead long before 1956. Text checked against the 1926 page images ('christmas Gift', 'christman Gifts.' as printed).

text:
Dear Peacock,
I received your feather with profound emotion. …

We have at present one cat, and twenty-four hens, who do nothing so vulgar as lay an egg, which checks the ice-cream tendency.

… The hills take off their purple frocks, and dress in long white nightgowns.

… Write, dear, when you feel like it.
Lovingly,
Emily.
title: To her cousin Louise Norcross
author: Emily Dickinson
story: Emily Dickinson to her young cousin Louise Norcross; Mabel Loomis Todd printed it in 1894, eight years after the poet’s death.

source.name: Letters of Emily Dickinson, ed. Todd (1894), vols. 1-2, Internet Archive full text

rights.basis: Dated by Todd '[December, 1861.]' (later editors suggest 1860); text from Todd's 1894 edition (US: before 1931). Author died 1886 (EU: life+70).

text:
Monna Margherita.
Io mando per lo vino della botte grande. Se vi fosse avanzato uno popone di stamane, prestatemelo. Sabato viene il mio vino di Valdinievole …

Io vi mando questo libro, che è de’ buoni. … Rimandatemelo a Firenze mercoledì, o giovidì, se potete … Salutate Francesco. …
Ser Lapo, in villa.
title: Lend me a melon
author: Ser Lapo Mazzei
recipient: Monna Margherita, wife of the merchant Francesco Datini, at Prato
story: A note sent from Grignano to borrow wine (and a melon) from the Datini household, printed by Cesare Guasti in 1880 among the notary’s letters.

source.name: Guasti (ed.), Lettere di un notaro a un mercante del secolo XIV (Florence, 1880), vol. II, p. 180, Internet Archive scan (text read from the page image)
source.licence: Public domain (pre-1931 printing; scan at the Internet Archive)

rights.basis: Grignano, 1395 (the editor suggests 29 September); first printed 1880 (US: before 1931). Writer died 1412 (EU: life+70).

text:
Dear Mrs. Coney,
Are you thinking I am lost, like the Babes in the Wood? Well, I am not …

We have the finest flock of Plymouth Rocks and get so many nice eggs. …

They have just three seasons here, winter and July and August. …

I think this letter is about to reach thirty-secondly, so I will send you my sincerest love and quit tiring you. …
Sincerely yours,
Elinore Rupert.
title: Three seasons in Wyoming
author: Elinore Rupert (later Elinore Pruitt Stewart)
recipient: Mrs. Coney, her former employer in Denver
story: Her first letter after the train and stage journey to Burnt Fork, written to the Denver woman she had once worked for; printed in Letters of a Woman Homesteader (1914), after a selection of the letters had appeared in The Atlantic Monthly.

source.name: Elinore Pruitt Stewart, Letters of a Woman Homesteader (Boston: Houghton Mifflin, May 1914), Project Gutenberg eBook #16623; checked against the 1914 Library of Congress scan (archive.org/details/lettersofwomanh00stew)
source.licence: Public domain (US; printed before 1931); Project Gutenberg transcription

rights.basis: Printed in 1914 (book; Atlantic Monthly 1913-14) (before 1931). Elinore Pruitt Stewart died in 1933 (before 1956). The publishers' note says the letters 'are printed as written, except for occasional omissions and the alteration of some of the names.'

text:
Al nome di Dio. A dì 11 di dicembre 1450.
Pel Favilla vetturale, che viene costà con some di Ghezzo della Casa, ti mando dodici marzolini de’ più begli s’è trovato qui in Firenze; e credo saranno buoni, secondo il saggio n’abbiàn fatto …

Ancora ti mando pel detto Favilla quattro camice e sei fazzoletti e uno isciugatoio. Guarda se le camice e l’altre cose ti piacciono …

Nè altro per questa. Iddio di male ti guardi.
Per la tua Alessandra, in Firenze.
title: To her son in Naples, with cheeses and shirts
author: Alessandra Macinghi Strozzi
story: One of the letters a Florentine widow wrote to her exiled sons, sent with a carrier in December 1450; printed by Cesare Guasti in 1877.

source.name: Lettere di una gentildonna fiorentina (1877), Internet Archive scan (checked against the page images)

rights.basis: Written 11 December 1450, first published 1877 (US: before 1931). Author died 1471 (EU: life+70).

text:
Dear Sir
This comes to inquire wither Mr. Henry J. Roberts of Liberia Monrovia West Africa, have Sent, to your care, for, me a Box containing one or more Gaires of Preserves, … If he has not Sent anything to your care for me, you will please to answer this, and If He has, Dear Sir, you will confer, a lasting favour on me to forward It Immediately, and Oblige yours, …
Mariah Fenemur
title: Has my box of preserves come?
author: Mariah Fenemur

writer.basis: Woodson's introduction says 'practically all of these letters were written by the Negroes themselves'; this one is in the section of letters by free Negroes to the American Colonization Society (running head 'The Mind of the Free Negro').

recipient: the Rev. William McLain, secretary of the American Colonization Society, Washington
story: Mariah Fenemur of Pittsfield, Massachusetts, wrote in March 1849 to ask the American Colonization Society whether a box of preserves sent to her from Monrovia had arrived; the letter stayed in the Society’s files until Carter G. Woodson printed it in 1925–26.

source.name: Carter G. Woodson (ed.), The Mind of the Negro as Reflected in Letters Written During the Crisis, 1800–1860 (Washington: Association for the Study of Negro Life and History, 1926); Internet Archive scan of the State Library of Pennsylvania copy, page images read
source.licence: Public domain in the US (published 1926; US term expired 1 January 2022). No licence statement on the IA item; the letters themselves pass by date (see rights).

rights.basis: US: first printed 1925 (JNH vol. X; the April 1925 issue text on the Internet Archive contains it), reprinted 1926; both before 1931. EU: an adult corresponding with Liberia in 1849, so born before about 1831; dead long before 1956. Published 1925, so any EU publication right (25 years) ended long ago. Text checked against the 1926 page images.

text:
Martin mio,
ya soy Pintor del Rey con quince mil reales, aunque no tengo tiempo te insinuaré como el Rey enbio orden a Bayeu y Maella que buscasen dos pintores lo mejor que se encontrase … Bayeu puso a su hermano y Maella a mi. Subio esta consulta al Rey y estubo echa la gracia y yo sin saber nada, que me cogio sin saber lo que me sucedia … y a Dios que ya te escribire.
Tuyo y retuyo.
title: To Martín Zapater: “I’m Painter to the King!”
author: Francisco de Goya

writer.basis: Born in Fuendetodos, Aragon.

story: Goya told his childhood friend Martín Zapater in Zaragoza about his royal appointment in July 1786; printed in 1868.

source.name: Goya: noticias biográficas (Zaragoza, Tip. La Académica reprint, c. 1928, of the 1868 text), p. 19, via Internet Archive (page scan read)

rights.basis: Written Madrid, 7 July 1786; first published 1868, reprinted before 1931 (US). Author died 1828 (EU: life+70).

text:
À Monsieur le
Directeur de la Poste de Londres.
J’ai cinquante trois ans. Veuillez être assez bon de me faire réponse pour me donner des résultats sur l’existence de Madame ——? Si parfois elle était toujours veuve je voudrais lui faire la proposition de lui demander sa main d’après que j’en aurais des nouvelles. En attendant, Monsieur, votre réponse.
title: Is Madame —— still a widow?
author: Unknown (a Frenchman aged 53; name not printed)
recipient: the Director of the London Post Office
dateNote: Undated; written by 1889, when J. W. Hyde printed it.
story: Sent to the Director of the London Post Office by a 53-year-old Frenchman who wanted to know whether a certain Madame was still living and still a widow, so that he could ask for her hand; Hyde printed it with her name blanked.

source.name: James Wilson Hyde, The Royal Mail: its Curiosities and Romance, 3rd ed. (London: Simpkin, Marshall, 1889; 1st ed. 1885), Project Gutenberg #39978, chapter XIX 'Curious letters addressed to the Post-office', p. 252
source.licence: Public domain (book printed 1889; Project Gutenberg: public domain in the USA)

rights.basis: US: printed by 1889 (before 1931). EU/UK: Hyde printed it anonymously (the writer's name and places are replaced by '——'), so the writer is not identifiable; anonymous work published before 1956. Written before 1889 (exact year unknown). Printed in the original French. The two-line address ('À Monsieur le / Directeur de la Poste de Londres.') is kept as printed.

text:
To the person in whose hands this message may fall,
I would like a correspondent in your city which I think would be of interest to each of us in the way of information.

… my age is 18. … It is snowing to-day; it is the first day of winter we have had. The thermometer is ten above zero. … Please state what day you receive this, as I would like to know how long a letter is on the road …
title: To the person in whose hands this message may fall
author: Unknown (an 18-year-old in Indiana; name not printed)
recipient: whoever the London Post Office chose to give it to
dateNote: Undated; written by 1889, when J. W. Hyde printed it.
story: Sent from Indiana to the General Post Office in London with an unsealed letter for any stranger who might like an American correspondent; Hyde printed it among the ‘social’ letters reaching St Martin’s-le-Grand.

source.name: James Wilson Hyde, The Royal Mail: its Curiosities and Romance, 3rd ed. (London: Simpkin, Marshall, 1889; 1st ed. 1885), Project Gutenberg #39978, chapter XIX, p. 253-254
source.licence: Public domain (book printed 1889; Project Gutenberg: public domain in the USA)

rights.basis: US: printed by 1889 (before 1931). EU/UK: Hyde printed it anonymously (the writer's name and places are replaced by '——'), so the writer is not identifiable; anonymous work published before 1956. Written before 1889 (exact year unknown). This is the enclosed letter. Cuts marked ' … ': 'My house is in the central part of the United States,'; the business, travel and Thanksgiving sentences; 'All business is suspended to-day.'; and the end of the last sentence ('—if you do not wish to answer this, please give to some of your friends who will—my address you will find on the enclosed card'). Hyde does not say whether it was ever passed on.

text: I never was better satisfied in my life, if I had only my dear relations and friends with me. … I have coffee in my lot, a good many other trees, and the guava, which makes nice sweetmeats. If I only had you and your family, mother and her family, and if my dear husband was returned, I should be as happy as the day is long.
title: As happy as the day is long
author: Eliza Hatter

writer.basis: Printed among 'Letters from Colonists' in Liberia; the editor says the writers were servants of the Blackburn sisters near Shepherdstown, Virginia, before their emigration.

story: Eliza Hatter, who had been enslaved by the Blackburn sisters near Shepherdstown, Virginia, before she emigrated to Liberia, wrote this to her sister; the American Colonization Society printed the extract in its African Repository in November 1832 under ‘Letters from Colonists’.

source.name: The African Repository and Colonial Journal, vol. VIII, no. 9 (November 1832), pp. 280–281; Internet Archive (Serials in Microfilm) scan, page image read
source.licence: Public domain (printed in the 1830s). No licence statement on the IA item; nothing in it is newly published.

rights.basis: US: printed 1832. EU: a married woman who had already emigrated and kept house in Liberia by 1832, so born before about 1813 and certainly dead long before 1956. Published 1832, so no publication right. Text checked against the page image (the OCR misreads 'I' as 'T' and 'is long' as 'islong').

text:
Ma chère amie,
Je profite de la commodité du citoyen Veyssiere, chef d’escadron de notre régiment qui part aujourd’hui pour la France, pour te donner de mes nouvelles, et en même tems pour te renouveller de nouveau le serment que je t’ai si souvent fait de t’aimer jusqu’à la mort. … Hélas! quand arrivera-t-il l’heureux moment d’une réunion si désirée ? …

Je finis, ma douce amie, en t’embrassant mille fois, et crois-moi pour la vie.
Ton fidel ami,
Dezirad
title: To Adeline in Marseille
author: Dezirad
story: Written in Cairo in August 1798, it was intercepted by Nelson’s fleet before it could reach Adeline in Marseille, and the British printed it in London in 1799 among the captured letters of Bonaparte’s army.

source.name: Correspondance intime de l'armée d'Égypte interceptée par la croisière anglaise, ed. Lorédan Larchey (Paris: R. Pincebourde, 1866), pp. 119-121
source.licence: Public domain (printed 1799 and 1866)

rights.basis: First printed 1799 in London (Copies of Original Letters from the Army of General Bonaparte in Egypt, Part the Second, J. Wright, French text with English translation; IA copy https://archive.org/details/bim_eighteenth-century_copies-of-original-lette_1799_1) and the same year in Paris (Correspondance de l'armee francaise en Egypte, Garnery, an VII; https://archive.org/details/32882019067670-correspondanced); text quoted from Larchey's 1866 Paris reprint (public domain). US: printed before 1931. EU: the writer was an adult serving in Egypt in 1798, so born before c.1780 and certainly dead long before 1956. No modern transcription used, so no publication right arises. OCR slip 't'aimejr' in the 1866 scan corrected to 't'aimer', as printed in the 1799 Paris edition.

text:
Lafayette, Ind.
Dear Santa Claus,
I am a little boy living with my grandma. I want you to bring me a drum, a wheelbarrow and a gun. If you will bring me all these I will be a real good little boy to my grandma.
Thanking you for all
I am yours——.
title: A drum, a wheelbarrow and a gun
author: Unknown (unsigned: 'I am yours——')
story: Never delivered to Santa: it was ‘rescued from the waste basket at the dead letter office’ in Washington and printed in the Evening Star on 20 December 1908.

text:
Anwyl Frawd,
Doe brydnhawn derbyniais ddau llythyr, un oddiwrth y brawd William … ag arall oddiwrthych chwithe, a diau mae odiaeth oedd clywed eich geiriau’ch deuwedd, ag megys mêl ir gwefusau ydynt imi yn y fangre aniddan honn, y man nad oes gennyf na chyfaill na châr a eill gymorth im ddifyrru y tywydd rhewlyd anwydog yma. …

Ni feddaf y tro yma iw chwanegu ond deisyf ar Dduw roddi llwyddiant ag iechyd i chwi, a blwyddyn newydd dda.
Eich caredigawl frawd,
Ioan Amhorys.
title: From Liverpool, to his brother Richard
author: John Morris (Ioan Morys)
story: Written from Liverpool in January 1739 by John Morris, an Anglesey sailor, to his brother Richard in London; printed in 1907 with the Morris brothers’ family letters.

source.name: Morris Letters, vol. I (1907), scan at the Internet Archive (text checked against page images pp. 15 and 18)

text:
Dear Madam,
I am happy in hearing that the bathing and drinking has been of real service to you.—I imagine you rise out of the waves another Venus—and could wish myself Neptune, to have the honor of escorting you to land.—Mr. P—— has sent me a pretty turtle, and in very good condition. … it will attend you at Privy Gardens, where (had turtles a sense of ambition) it would think itself happy in its destination.
I am, dear Madam,
Your much obliged,
humble servant,
Ign. Sancho.
title: To Mrs. C——, with a turtle
author: Ignatius Sancho

writer.basis: His letters were printed in 1782 as 'Letters of the Late Ignatius Sancho, an African'.

story: Ignatius Sancho, born on a slave ship and later a Westminster shopkeeper, sent this with a turtle in August 1775; printed in 1782, two years after his death.

source.name: Letters of the Late Ignatius Sancho, an African, 3rd ed. (London: J. Nichols, 1784), via Project Gutenberg

rights.basis: Written 14 Aug. 1775; first published 1782 (US: before 1931). Author died 1780 (EU: life+70).

text:
Ryght reverent and wurschypfull, and my ryght welebeloved Voluntyne, I recomande me unto yowe … And yf it please yowe to here of my welefar, I am not in good heele of body, nor of herte, nor schall be tyll I her ffrom yowe …

But yf that ye loffe me, as I tryste verely that ye do, ye will not leffe me therefor …

And thys letter was indyte at Topcroft, with full hevy herte, &c.
By your own,
Margery Brews
title: To my right well-beloved Valentine
author: Margery Brews
story: Margery Brews wrote this at Topcroft in February 1477, days before St Valentine’s Day, to John Paston, whom she calls her ‘Voluntyne’ while their parents argued over her dowry; Gairdner thinks they married that August.

source.name: The Paston Letters, ed. James Gairdner (1904), vol. V, letter 897 (Project Gutenberg #42239)
source.licence: Public domain (printed 1787/1904; Project Gutenberg e-text, public domain in the USA)

text:
M. M. V. V.!
Reeds bijna elf maanden zijn er voorbij gegaan, zonder iets van u of betrekkelijk u of ons verlaten vaderland te vernemen …

Gaarne zou ik met u, mijne vrienden! nog verder voortkouten … Inderdaad maakt het sluiten van mijn’ brief bijna denzelfden indruk op mij, als of ik voorheen in eenen vriendenkring mijne pijp moest nederleggen, om mij gereed te maken het gezelschap te verlaten.
Leeft wel!
K. Jz. Beukma.
title: Like laying down my pipe
author: K. Jz. Beukma
recipient: his family and friends in the province of Groningen
story: Written on his Indiana farm on 8 July 1837 and printed unchanged in Groningen in 1838, because his family and friends had asked for his letters home to be published.

text: Not having received the live bullfinch mentioned by you as having arrived at the Returned-letter office two days ago, having been posted as a letter contrary to the regulations of the postal system, I now write to ask you to have the bird fed and forwarded at once to —— … I shall write to the Postmaster-General, who is a very intimate friend of my father’s … This is not an idle threat, so you will oblige by following the above instructions.
title: The live bullfinch
author: Unknown (a schoolboy; name not printed)

text:
Amado hijo de mi alma y de mi corazón:
… He visto que tienes maestro de música y de baile … dime si tocaste algún instrumento en esa grande orquesta … y dime si hablas corriente el francés con las madamas. ¡Cuánto diera por verte detrás de una cortina en esas concurrencias y oirte! …

Dios quiera … que tenga el gusto de volverte á ver tu madre, que te ama como á su vida y cuanto puede.
J. María Manuela
title: To hide behind a curtain and hear you
author: María Manuela (Doña María Manuela Pignatelli de Aragón y Gonzaga, Duchess of Villahermosa)
recipient: her son, the Duke of Villahermosa, then in France
story: Written from Madrid on 15 April (the book’s footnote dates it to the spring before the battle of Vitoria, i.e. 1813) to her son, who was living in France, and printed by her family’s biographer from the Villahermosa archive in 1896.

source.name: Ortí y Brull, Doña María Manuela Pignatelli ... Duquesa de Villahermosa, tomo II (1896), Internet Archive scan doamaramanue02orti (University of Toronto copy)

text:
My Dear Wife
I have took the first opportunity that I had to write these few lines to you … I hope you will take great care of yourself do not climb over yonder fence to often do not roam through yonder woods to often do not walk over yonder feilds to often but take care of yourself and remember what I told you before you left home. and in the mean time I remain yours and you mine as long as life remains
Your affectionate husband
John Miller Jr
title: Do not climb over yonder fence
author: John Miller Jr

writer.basis: Woodson's introduction says 'practically all of these letters were written by the Negroes themselves'; printed in his section of 'Letters Largely Personal or Private'.

recipient: his wife, Anne Miller, visiting her mother at Newport, Delaware
story: Written from Philadelphia on 9 June 1833 by John Miller Jr. to his wife Anne, who was visiting her mother at Newport, Delaware; printed by Carter G. Woodson in 1926.

text:
Hiærtelskede kiære Kone og Søn.
Jeg maa herved lade Eder vide hvor ledes ieg lever … ieg og Lensmanden er Senge kammerrater, Her er meget Snille Folk, vi faar kaffe om Morgenen i qvarteret …

— tiiden er ude vi skal møde hils alle venner …
C. Hoen
Til kiære Kone og Børn — — i Hast
title: A farmer at the 1814 Constitutional Assembly writes home
author: Christopher Bergersen Hoen
story: Written home on 13 April 1814 by a farmer from Øvre Eker while he sat in the Eidsvoll assembly that wrote Norway’s constitution; printed in Historisk Tidsskrift in 1901.

source.name: Historisk Tidsskrift 1901, via Norwegian Wikisource (raw transcription, checked against the page scans)

rights.basis: Written 13 April 1814 (Lysager, Eidsvoll), first published 1901 (US: before 1931). Author died 1845 (EU: life+70).

text:
Dear Father and Mother and little John.
… Thank God that I am in a state of health at present, and as happy as any person in the world; and I hope you are all the same. … I was glad to step my foot on land again. I had 1lb. of beef steak and 2 quarts of cider …

Tell little John, that he must grow as fast as he can, and come to me …
John Stedman.
title: Tell little John to grow
author: John Stedman
recipient: his parents and his little brother John at Hascombe, Surrey
story: Written in August 1832 after a long journey from Quebec, partly on foot, to Kettle Creek, where he hired himself to a farmer for a year; printed with other emigrants’ letters by the Petworth Emigration Committee in 1833.

text:
Para entregarle a los Reyes Magos lo más pronto posible.

Después de desearles que vengan buenos y contentos, les pido que me traigan una linda y preciosa muñeca con cabellos negros como los míos y que cierre los ojitos y a mi querida hermanita una maquinita para que me cosa los vestiditos … esa preciosa muñequita y esa querida maquinita que la vamos a guardar hasta cuando tengamos 20 años. …

Reyes Magos benditos, acordate de mí. Me llamo Julia …

Reyes no te olvides de nosotras; sé bueno.
title: We’ll keep them till we’re twenty
author: Unknown (gives her name only as 'Julia')
recipient: the Reyes Magos, via the editor of Crítica
story: One of the children’s letters to the Three Kings that Crítica printed on 5 January 1924, the day the paper’s lorries handed out free toys to children across Buenos Aires.

source.name: Diario Crítica, 5 Jan 1924 (no. 4035), page 6, Internet Archive scan BNA_S001181802_19240105N04035 (image 6)

text:
Má nejmilejší paní, paní Sylvičko!
Svými službami se ti poroučím a ruku líbám. … S tím sem tvá jako svá, buď zatím veselá a když jsi smutná zpomeň na mne, nebo vím, že jsi víceji veselá nežli smutná. S tím se ti poroučím se všemi svými i s Paclem. Pacel měl na miliony blech když z Prahy přijel. Přála bych sobě na tejden mezi vámi býti.
Tvá dědičná poddaná a služebnice
Kateřina L.
title: To her friend Sylvie: be cheerful
author: Kateřina L.
story: An undated note to her friend Sylvie Černínová (strawberries went to the count, none to her), printed in 1869 in František Dvorský’s collection of old letters by Czech women.

source.name: Dvorský, Staré písemné památky žen a dcer českých (1869), e-book of the Prague City Library (MKP), checked against the 1869 page scan at the Internet Archive (pp. 293–294)

text:
Sir
My ffather is under the Rasor: Therefore He has commanded me to present his humble duty to you, and to Let you Know that he will waite on you at dinner and so will also,
Your most Dutyfull Grandson and humble Servant
Edmund Verney
title: My father is under the razor
author: Edmund Verney
story: Mun Verney sent this note between the two Verney houses at Claydon around 1687, while his father was being shaved; the 1899 memoir prints it as ‘a note of Mun’s to his grandfather’ that survived.

text:
Theuerste Eltern Geschwistern und Freunde!
Um noch einmahl an die Heimath zurück zu denken, kann ich nicht unterlassen an Euch zu schreiben … Liebe Eltern und Geschwister ich sehne mich doch einmahl zurück … ich bin jetzt bei einem Gärtner und bekomme das Monat 25 Thlr. und das Essen. Das Klima ist sehr warm im Sommer, man kann im August nicht in Betten schlafen, dann schläft man draußen, der Amerikaner hat keine Federbetten sondern lauter wollene Decken. … ich verbleibe Euer getreuer Sohn und Bruder bis in den Tod. …
M. L. H.
title: No feather beds in America
author: Unknown (signed 'M. L. H.')
recipient: his parents, brothers and sisters and friends in Pomerania
story: Written in St. Louis on 3 August 1838 by an emigrant from Pomerania and printed in 1839 by a church paper, then reprinted in a Stralsund weekly, which kept his own spelling.

text:
Dear Santa Claus:
Will you please bring me a few presents? I want a Teddy bear, a piano, a box of paints, a box of tools, a sister, a chair, a pair of mittens.
Merry Christmas to you from
C. B.

author: Unknown (signed 'C. B.')

text:
Honored Sir:
Three years have elapsed since I first promised to you faithfully, that I would write to you of my health and situation … I have quite a flourishing school of about seventy children … I have some native girls that learn very fast. All of them are spelling—three of them are writing—and one of them is quite fond of composing letters. …

I hope I shall soon hear from you and the family, as I often think of the little girls. …
Your most obedient servant,
Elizabeth Thompson
title: One of them is fond of composing letters
author: Elizabeth Thompson

text:
Můj nejmilejší pane bratříčku!
Přeji vám na pánu Bohu všecko nejlepší dobré nic jinače než jako sama sobě. Tu vám dvanácte facalítův posílám, pán Bůh rač dáti, abyste je v dobrém zdraví spotřebovali; chtěla jsem je vám dáti po všech čtyřech stranách šiti, ale bojím se, žeby jich ani do roku neušili … až sobě koupíte nizozemského plátna, dám je vám pěkněji ušiti. …
Marie Anna Trmalová z Chyš a z Egrbergu.
title: To her brother, with twelve handkerchiefs
author: Marie Anna Trmalová z Chyš
recipient: her brother, Šťastný Václav Pětipeský z Chyš
story: Sent with a dozen handkerchiefs to her brother in November 1613; kept in the family archive at Roudnice and printed by František Dvorský in 1869.

text:
Excelentísimos monarcas:
Nuestras hermanitas … esperan de Ss. Ms. los siguientes regalos que vosotros ofrecéis en este mágico día:

… La Ignacia, como es un poco pernilarga y tiene unas manos especiales para tocar el piano, pide un pianito para poder ensayar un shimmy (música de moda).

… Nuestras hermanitas esperan ansiosas vuestros regalos … para que lleguéis pronto a nuestra casa con vuestros mágicos camiones y camellos cargados de juguetes …
Mary y Nelly
title: A pianito for the shimmy
author: Unknown (signed 'Mary y Nelly'; first names only)
recipient: the Reyes Magos (Baltasar, Melchor and Gaspar), via the editor of Crítica

text:
Dear Friends,
This comes with our kind love to you all … We have got a cow. Father gave 30 dollars for her. … Father says he would not come back to England again for no respects. …

I hope you will excuse my bad writing. If any comes, which I hope you will, please to bring some dried yeast, for there is none here: we wet our flour, and bake it on the ashes. … So God bless you all.

text:
Monna Margherita.
Io sono venuto in villa a vedere uno lavorio che fa monna Bartola. …

Io sono alla lucente e lieta aria iscalzo: e fammi venire sonno il suono de’ coregiati, e l’aie nette e pulite m’invitano a saltare e fare tomi ischiavoneschi in sulle montagne de’ grassi grani … Qui non à cicale nè mosconi o tarantole … Sono solo …
Il secondo fattore iscrisse questa.
title: Barefoot at the threshing
author: Ser Lapo Mazzei
recipient: Monna Margherita, wife of the merchant Francesco Datini, at Prato
story: Written at harvest time from his country house to his friend’s wife in Prato, signed with a joke, and first printed in 1910 for the 500th anniversary of Francesco Datini’s death.

text:
Muy ilustre Señora, mi Señora:
… Pues ¿qué os pudiera contar, Señora, de los secretos naturales que he descubierto estando guisando? Veo que un huevo se une y fríe en la manteca o aceite y, por contrario, se despedaza en el almíbar … pero, señora, ¿qué podemos saber las mujeres sino filosofías de cocina? … Y yo suelo decir viendo estas cosillas: Si Aristóteles hubiera guisado, mucho más hubiera escrito. …
B. V. M. vuestra más favorecida
Juana Inés de la Cruz

Kjære forældre og søskende!
Jeg skriver nu til eder fra en stor by, som hedder Minneapolis …

Kjøkkenet mit er rart, kan dere tro, og stort er det ikke, men jeg kan ikke sige andet end at det er ubegribelig letvint at stelle i, nu da jeg er vant til det. …

Fruen sa, at jeg maa ta bad engang om ugen, og det var rart i det første, men nu synes jeg det er noksaa godt. …

Men nu faar jeg slutte dette mit brev med flittig hilsen til — — — — — — —
Mathea . . .

text:
Mr. Still:—Dear Sir— …
I arrived in New Bedford Thursday morning safely and what little I have seen of the city I like it very much my friends were very glad to see me. I found my sister very well. … It might been supposed, out of sight out of mind, but it is not so. I never forget my friends. … Kiss your dear little children for me. …
I still remain your friend,
Ellen Saunders.

With much love to you,
Elinore.

Apreciable director del popular diario CRITICA.
Después de desearle muchas felicidades en año Nuevo, le diré que yo soy un lectorcito de los chistes de CRITICA y apenas tengo 8 años.

Desearía que como su diario es tan popular, mi mayor desea sería que usted se dignara hacer llegar mis ruegos a los señores Reyes Magos que estoy ansiando el día 6 de enero … un manomóvil para mí, una muñeca para mi hermanita y una para Mingo, Julio y Lucía.

Lieber, was ich mich und das Kind freuen auf das gute Väterchen, kannst Du Dir nicht vorstellen, und wir streiten uns des Morgens im Bette, wer Dich zuerst grüßen will. … Heute gehe in die “Zauberflöte” zum 30. C.

Dear Master,
I take the liberty to write to you myself … that you may know Columbine and I are quite well, and play about as usual. …

This morning I have seen a note from you, which says you will come to-morrow. Columbine and I are extremely happy to hear it; for then there will be some dinner to come and go on. Being to see you so soon, no more at present from your
Obedient little dog,
Nero.

text:
I have a goodly number of pupils … I have some very interesting little girls, who have endeared themselves to me by a thousand tender ties. I have watched them from the alphabet to more interesting things. I have seen them trying to point out the different countries on the map … My dear sister, you cannot imagine what my feelings are sometimes, when seated in my little piazza, listening to their little pious talk.
I remain yours, in the bonds of christian love, forever,
Eunice Moore.

Bring your home-made wine; a few apples … Bring your tea kettle. … So no more at present from your dutiful son and daughter,
George & Lydia Hilton.

text:
My Dear Lewis:
Pardon my negligence in allowing so many weeks to pass away without writing and accept this tardy letter. …

Spring has brought with it as usual, the ever dreaded, yearly school examinations … Monday I thought of nothing but Chloride of Sodium, Nitrate of Silver detection of arsenic, uses of Zinc etc etc; Tuesday, Parlez-vous français? … yesterday oh! terrible thought Plane Trigonometry; do you wonder then that last night I dreamed of being in France? …
Yours truly
H. Amelia Loguen.
title: Exams, and a dream of France
author: H. Amelia Loguen

Dear, dear Friend,
Can you guess how happy I am? Be it ever so humble there is no place like home.

It is so good to sit in my creaky old rocker, to hold Junior, to feel his dear weight … Some young calves have come while we were gone; a whole squirming nest full of little pigs. My chickens have outgrown my knowledge. …

I will write you again soon.
Your happy friend,
E. R. S.

Mon bon ami,
Je suis bien aise que tu aimes tes cravates. Tu les appelles des cadeaux! Je ne t’en ai jamais fait qu’un, que j’apprécie beaucoup, qui est bien à toi et qui est aussi à moi …

Je te trouve bien pastoral d’aller lire mes lettres dans les prés; j’ai peur que tu ne les sèmes en chemin … Si je te connaissais plus soigneux, combien je te confierais de jolies choses! Tu saurais que je t’aime bien, que j’ai grande envie de te revoir …
Julie.

Any kind of seed you plant will grow; and as for corn, and such things, I have never seen a better place for raising them.

Dear Uncle and Aunt,
I take this opportunity of writing to you … I am doing very well; working at the carpenter and joiner’s trade, this two years … Jane and Harriet are grown fine girls; and I expect the family will be grown out of knowledge, except me, and I am the same little runt as ever. I forgot to tell you, that mother had a young baby, about four months old. … So no more at present, from your ever affectionate nephew, and grandson,
Alexander Hilton.

Jesus
Sea con vuestra merced. Da tan poco lugar Serna, que no querria alargarme, y no sé acabar, cuando comienzo á escribir á vuestra merced …
